key_recommendations: If a patient is scheduled to receive an ICD and is in sinus rhythm with a left bundle branch block (LBBB), consider CRT-D if QRS is 130–149 ms and recommend if QRS ≥150 ms. Choice between CRT-P and CRT-D may depend on clinical judgement and indication (symptom relief vs mortality benefit).
When LVEF is reduced, RV pacing may exacerbate dyssynchrony; CRT is preferred over RV pacing for patients with HFrEF who have an indication for ventricular pacing to reduce morbidity.
Patients with a conventional pacemaker or ICD who develop worsening heart failure with a high proportion of RV pacing despite optimal medical therapy should be considered for upgrading to CRT.

AF is not in itself an indication for AV node ablation in patients with CRT, except selectively when ventricular rate remains persistently high despite pharmacological control. CRT may be superior to RV pacing in patients undergoing AV node ablation.
Ensure a high proportion of biventricular pacing; observational data suggest prognosis worsens when biventricular capture is <98%, although this has not been confirmed in randomized trials.
Extensive myocardial scar is associated with less improvement in LV function with CRT and higher pacing thresholds; lead placement should avoid scarred regions where possible.

Imaging tests for dyssynchrony were historically of limited value; two novel markers (apical rocking and septal flash) have been associated with CRT response but are not validated as selection criteria in randomized trials.
Optimization of AV or VV intervals after implantation (by echo or ECG criteria or blood pressure response) is uncertain but may be considered in patients with a disappointing response to CRT.
Review diuretic therapy after CRT implantation and consider dose reduction or discontinuation if appropriate; CRT implantation may allow further optimization of medical therapy for HFrEF.
evidence_notes: Only one randomized trial compared CRT-P vs CRT-D and showed no difference in morbidity or mortality, but was not powered for such a difference.
DANISH study in NICM patients (58% received CRT) showed no subgroup suggestion that CRT-P was inferior to CRT-D.
Subgroup analyses (e.g., RAFT) did not show outcome differences between CRT and RV pacing in some contexts; evidence for AF patients is limited and conflicting.
Observational studies report associations between biventricular capture <98% and worse prognosis; causal mechanism uncertain and unconfirmed in randomized data.
Novel imaging markers (apical rocking, septal flash) associated with CRT response but not tested as selection criteria in RCTs.
patient_groups_considered: Patients receiving ICD with LBBB in sinus rhythm
Patients with reduced LVEF and indication for ventricular pacing (HFrEF)
Patients with conventional pacemaker/ICD who develop worsening HF with high RV pacing burden
Patients with AF with high persistent ventricular rate despite drugs (selective consideration for AV node ablation + CRT)
Patients with extensive myocardial scar (consider lead placement avoiding scar)
practical_considerations: Choice between CRT-P and CRT-D may be individualized; only limited randomized data comparing them
Attempt to maximize biventricular pacing percentage; investigate causes of low capture (device programming, lead placement, myocardial disease)
Avoid placing leads in scarred myocardium where possible due to higher thresholds and less improvement
Consider AV/ VV interval optimization in non-responders using echo/ECG/BP-guided methods or in a specialist practical article referenced
content.references_summary: Multiple trials and observational studies are cited (including DANISH, RAFT and small trials) and several guideline/practical articles referenced regarding optimization and response predictors.
